readingInstruction: Read Matthew 19:1-20:34. Jesus teaches on marriage, children, and wealth, then tells the parable of the workers in the vineyard. He predicts his death a third time and heals two blind men. Read 20:25-28 slowly.
settingTheScene: Jesus has left Galilee and is traveling toward Jerusalem. Along the road, he teaches about the shape of kingdom life: faithfulness in marriage, welcome for the vulnerable, freedom from the grip of money, and a radical idea of greatness. The shadow of the cross grows longer, and the disciples still do not understand.
observation: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate” (19:6).
“Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven” (19:14).
“If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (19:21).
“It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God” (19:24).
“With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible” (19:26).
“But many who are first will be last, and the last first” (19:30).
“Are you envious because I am generous?” (20:15).
“Whoever would be great among you must be your servant… even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (20:26-28).
interpretation:
On marriage, Jesus goes back to Genesis. God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh. Divorce was permitted by Moses because of hardness of hearts, but it was not the original design. Jesus takes marriage seriously, as a covenant joined by God.

When parents bring children for blessing, the disciples try to send them away. Jesus rebukes them. The kingdom belongs to those who receive it with a child’s openness and dependence.

The rich young man is a tragic scene. He has kept the commandments, and he asks what he still lacks. Jesus lovingly tests his heart: sell what you have, give to the poor, and follow me. The man goes away sorrowful, for he had great wealth. His possessions had hold of him. Jesus tells the disciples how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom, and when they ask who can be saved, he says, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” Salvation is a gift of God’s power, not something we manage. Peter asks what the disciples will get, and Jesus promises great reward, and then warns that the first will be last.

The vineyard parable makes the point. Workers hired at the last hour receive the same pay as those who worked all day. The owner says, “Are you envious because I am generous?” God’s grace is not wages. It is a gift.

Then comes the third prediction of death, and immediately two disciples ask for the best seats. Jesus redefines greatness. In the world, leaders lord it over others. In the kingdom, the great one serves. And he gives himself as the model: the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many. This is the key to the Gospel.
connection: Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 are quoted in 19:4-5. Mark 10:17-31 gives a parallel to the rich young ruler. Philippians 2:5-8 describes the servant-hearted mind of Christ. 1 Timothy 6:17-19 teaches the rich to be generous. Isaiah 53:10-12 describes the suffering servant who bears the sin of many. 1 Peter 1:18-19 says we were ransomed by the precious blood of Christ. Ephesians 2:8-9 says salvation is a gift of God, not a result of works.
application:
Ask what you would find hardest to give up if Jesus asked. Pray about it honestly.

Welcome a child or a person of low status this week in a way that costs you something.

Practice servant leadership in one place where you have influence: at home, at work, or at church.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for giving his life as a ransom for you.
Ask him to free you from the love of money or status.
Ask him to teach you to serve.
